mcqs.question: In a chat room with five users where every user holds direct references to every other user, what happens when a sixth user joins?
options: Nothing needs to change — new users automatically discover existing ones
The chat room's message format must be redefined from scratch
All five existing users need to be updated to hold a reference to the new sixth user
Only the newest user needs any code changes
mcqs.explanation: A full mesh of direct references means every existing participant must be updated to know about a new one, since connections aren't automatic — this n-squared growth in connections is exactly the coupling problem Mediator eliminates by routing everything through one hub instead. No message format change or single-user-only update is implied by adding a mesh connection.

mcqs.question: A `ChatRoom` mediator grows to also handle message persistence, spam filtering, user permissions, and notification delivery. What does this signal?
options: This is ideal — a mediator should absorb as much responsibility as possible to keep other objects decoupled
Mediator pattern is no longer being used once a class has more than one method
This is only a problem if the class exceeds a specific line count defined by the pattern
The mediator has become a god object; coordination and unrelated concerns should be separated into their own collaborators
mcqs.explanation: Centralizing communication is meant to reduce mesh coupling, not to make the mediator absorb every unrelated concern — when it does, the coupling just relocates into one oversized class instead of disappearing. There's no fixed line-count threshold that defines the pitfall, and having multiple methods doesn't by itself indicate the problem.

mcqs.question: In the Memento pattern, why does the `History` (caretaker) class store `EditorMemento` objects without ever calling `getContent()` on them?
options: Because getContent() is deprecated and should never be called by any class
Because JavaScript/TypeScript classes cannot expose methods to more than one caller
So the caretaker manages only the timing of saves/restores, while only the originator that created a memento meaningfully interprets its contents, preserving encapsulation
Because mementos are read-only and getContent() would throw an error if called externally
mcqs.explanation: The caretaker is deliberately kept ignorant of a memento's actual contents — it only manages when to push/pop snapshots — while the originator retains sole meaningful access to what's inside, which is exactly what keeps Memento from breaking encapsulation. Nothing here is about deprecation, a method-caller limit, or the call throwing an error.

mcqs.question: A drawing app's canvas state is a large bitmap that has no natural 'inverse operation' for most edits. Which undo approach fits better, and why?
options: Command-based undo, because computing an inverse action is always straightforward regardless of the operation
Memento-based undo — snapshotting the state directly is simpler when a clean inverse operation isn't naturally definable
Neither approach can support undo for bitmap-based editing
Command-based undo, because it never requires any memory for storing history
mcqs.explanation: When actions don't have a cheap, natural inverse (unlike inserting/deleting text), snapshotting the whole relevant state with Memento is the more practical choice, even at higher memory cost. Command-based undo assumes inverses are easy to compute, which isn't true for arbitrary bitmap edits, and Command still requires storing action history in memory.
